subQuestions.questionText: The value of skills owned by the entrepreneur and used in the production process is called … cost.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – implicit (2 marks)
Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using resources owned by the entrepreneur (such as their own skills or labour) for which no direct monetary payment is made.

subQuestions.questionText: A situation where it is impossible to increase the welfare of one individual without making another worse off is called … efficiency.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – Pareto (2 marks)
Pareto efficiency is a state of allocation where no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.

subQuestions.questionText: The demand curve for an oligopolist is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – kinked (2 marks)
The oligopolist faces a kinked demand curve because rivals follow price decreases but not price increases, which tends to keep prices stable.

subQuestions.questionText: Income enjoyed by producers of goods is known as … benefit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – private (2 marks)
A private benefit is the benefit (income) that accrues directly to the producer of a good, as opposed to a social or external benefit enjoyed by third parties.

subQuestions.questionText: An inflation rate that excludes items with highly volatile prices is called … inflation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – core (2 marks)
Core inflation excludes volatile items such as food and fuel to reveal the underlying, more stable inflation trend.

subQuestions.questionText: Religious events are included under … tourism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – cultural (2 marks)
Religious events and pilgrimages form part of cultural tourism, which involves visiting places for their cultural, historical or religious significance.

subQuestions.questionText: The process of converting waste material into economic goods is known as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – recycling (2 marks)
Recycling converts waste material back into usable economic goods, reducing pollution and conserving resources.

subQuestions.questionText: Public sector intervention that allows businesses to sell their licences to other businesses is called …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – marketable permits (2 marks)
Marketable (tradable) permits allow businesses to buy and sell the right to pollute or produce, using the market to control environmental damage.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the item in COLUMN A with the correct description from COLUMN B. Item: Long run. (COLUMN B options: A) an international agreement aimed at reducing greenhouse gases; B) represents the cost of an average basket of goods and services; C) products that are eco-friendly and can be absorbed by the environment without any harm; D) people travelling through South Africa to get to another destination; E) each business must take the actions of others into account; F) all factors of production are variable; G) income received from selling one extra unit of output; H) quantities change without a change in the price; I) a market structure that is dominated by two businesses)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: F – all factors of production are variable (1 mark)
In the long run there are no fixed factors of production; all inputs can be varied.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Marginal revenue.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: G – income received from selling one extra unit of output (1 mark)
Marginal revenue is the additional revenue earned from selling one more unit of output.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Duopoly.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: I – a market structure that is dominated by two businesses (1 mark)
A duopoly is an oligopoly in which two firms dominate the market.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Perfectly elastic demand curve.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: H – quantities change without a change in the price (1 mark)
A perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve means any quantity can be sold at the given price, so quantity changes while price stays constant.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Consumer price index.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – represents the cost of an average basket of goods and services (1 mark)
The CPI measures the cost of a representative basket of consumer goods and services over time.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Transit tourists.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – people travelling through South Africa to get to another destination (1 mark)
Transit tourists pass through a country en route to a final destination elsewhere.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Kyoto Protocol.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – an international agreement aimed at reducing greenhouse gases (1 mark)
The Kyoto Protocol is an international treaty committing countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Biodegradable.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – products that are eco-friendly and can be absorbed by the environment without any harm (1 mark)
Biodegradable products break down naturally and are absorbed by the environment without causing harm.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A situation where the market supplies goods that match the needs of the consumers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Allocative efficiency (1 mark)
Allocative efficiency occurs when resources are used to produce the goods and services that consumers actually want.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A market structure that consists of many businesses selling differentiated products.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Monopolistic competition (1 mark)
Under monopolistic competition many firms sell similar but differentiated products.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Goods that are seen to be socially harmful.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Demerit (goods) (1 mark)
Demerit goods (e.g. cigarettes, alcohol) are considered socially harmful and are often over-consumed in a free market.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Prices of goods and services that continuously decrease over a long period of time.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Deflation (1 mark)
Deflation is a sustained decrease in the general price level over a long period.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Monetary policy approach used by the SARB to keep price changes within 3–6%.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Inflation targeting (1 mark)
Inflation targeting is the SARB's monetary policy framework aimed at keeping inflation within the 3–6% target band.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The variety of plant and animal life within an ecosystem.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Biodiversity (1 mark)
Biodiversity refers to the variety of plant and animal life found within an ecosystem.

subQuestions.questionText: State any TWO objectives of the competition policy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct objective (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Prevent monopolies from abusing their power.
• Regulate the formation of mergers and acquisitions by firms wishing to exercise market power.
• To stop firms from using restrictive practices like fixing prices or dividing markets.
(Accept any other relevant and correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is a monopolistic competitive market regarded as a hybrid market structure?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2 = 2 marks):
It is a combination of a monopoly and perfect competition (market).

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the cartoon 'BARRIERS TO ENTRY' in the question paper. The cartoon shows barriers such as Investment Capital, Branding, Intellectual Property and Patents, and Regulations and Licences.) In the above cartoon, identify a barrier to entry used by a monopolistic competitor to increase its market share.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Investment capital / Branding (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the type of monopoly that is characterised by the use of patents.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Artificial / legal (monopoly) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term economies of scale.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
Economies of scale occur when output increases by more than the percentage increase in inputs / when the cost per unit decreases as output expands.
(Accept any other relevant and correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: How would barriers to entry influence profits in the market?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
New businesses are restricted from entering the market, so existing businesses will enjoy economic profit in both the short run and the long run.
(Accept any other relevant and correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is it a challenge for monopolies to charge excessively high prices?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• A monopoly is limited by market demand and consumers may stop buying if prices are too high.
• Consumers have limited budgets, therefore monopolies cannot charge excessive prices.
• The monopolist's product still has to compete for consumers' favour with all other products in the economy.
• Price increases are sometimes regulated by the government to protect the consumer.
(Accept any other relevant and correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the graphs 'Industry/Market' and 'Individual business' in the question paper. The individual-business graph shows MC, AC and a horizontal D=AR=MR line, with quantities q1, q2 and q3 on the horizontal axis.) Identify the quantity where the individual business will maximise profit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: q2 (1 mark)
Profit is maximised where MC = MR.

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the graphs in the question paper.) Name the market structure illustrated above.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Perfect (competition / market) (1 mark)
The horizontal D=AR=MR curve for the individual business indicates a perfect market.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term economic profit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
Economic profit occurs when a firm's total revenue exceeds total costs / when price (AR) is greater than average cost / the profit made by the business over and above normal profit.
(Accept any other relevant and correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why does the individual business take the price determined by the industry?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• An individual firm is very small in relation to the industry and has no influence over the market price.
• If individual firms charge higher prices, they may lose customers or market share.
• When firms charge lower prices, they can incur losses.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How would the entry of new firms in the industry impact the individual business in the long run?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• Competition will increase as the number of competitors in the market increases.
• Supply of goods and services will increase, leading to lower prices.
• Lower prices will reduce economic profit, and the individual business will make only normal profit in the long run.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a graph, explain the relationship between marginal revenue and the demand curve (AR) of a monopoly.
subQuestions.memoText:
GRAPH – Marginal revenue and average revenue (Max 4 marks):
• Correct drawing and labelling of the MR curve – 1 mark
• Correct drawing and labelling of the AR/dd curve – 1 mark
• Correct positioning of MR and AR/dd relative to the axes – 1 mark
• Labelling of axes (Price/Revenue on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis) – 1 mark

EXPLANATION (Max 4 marks):
• The marginal revenue curve, with the exception of the first unit, will lie below the dd/AR curve.
• The demand curve (AR) is negatively sloping, which results in more goods being sold at a lower price, hence the additional revenue (MR) will decrease as well.
• The MR curve intersects the horizontal axis at a point halfway between the origin and the AR curve.
• The monopolist will always set a price above point A on the AR curve, because marginal revenue will be positive.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.) Maximum 4 marks.

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse measures that may be used by the government to promote competition in the economy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained measure). Government can promote competition by:
• initiating a dedicated national inspectorate that deals with the monitoring and enforcement of competition policies.
• integrating competition policy with national policy objectives such as industrial and macroeconomic policies.
• reforming and strengthening monopoly laws directed at anti-competitive conduct.
• reviewing current practices and regulations in corporate governance / reducing red-tape / deregulating to make it easier for new businesses to operate.
• ensuring that previously disadvantaged people have an equal opportunity to participate in the economy.
• allowing imports to increase competition on local products, thereby forcing local business to keep their prices low.
• attracting foreign direct investment to increase competition in local markets.
• promoting small and micro enterprises (entrepreneurship) to increase competition on large businesses and increase supply of goods in the economy.
• implementing the competition policy to reduce anti-competitive behaviour such as price fixing by oligopolies and monopolies.
• decreasing the cost of doing business in South Africa.
• decreasing corporate tax to encourage new businesses to enter the market.
• upgrading, maintaining and providing sufficient infrastructure in which businesses can operate.
• offering subsidies for skills development to encourage entrepreneurship.
• fining businesses for anti-competitive behaviour.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: State any TWO criteria for an activity to be regarded as tourism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct criterion (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Purpose of the visit
• No remuneration
• Minimum of one night
• Maximum of one year
• Travelling distance of more than 160 km
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is it important to focus on preservation worldwide?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2 = 2 marks):
• Preservation ensures that natural resources are kept intact and can still be used by future generations.
• Ecological systems, heritage sites, wetlands, birds, flowers, etc. need to be preserved to avoid extinction.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the graph 'IMPACT OF COVID-19 ON INBOUND TOURISTS – TOURISM SALES' in the question paper. The graph plots the number of tourists (in '000) per month from December 2019 to November 2020.) Name the factor that caused a sharp decrease in tourism sales between January and April 2020.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Covid-19 pandemic / lockdown restrictions (1 mark)
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE reason why the government imposes tax on tourist activities.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark:
• Raise revenue.
• To improve tourist attraction sites / maintain infrastructure.
• Recover external costs.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term inbound tourist.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
Tourists from other countries who come to visit South Africa.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the role played by tourism in infrastructure development in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Development of the tourism sector leads to improvement of social infrastructure in the form of hospitals, public protection services, information services, etc.
• The tourism sector plays an important role in the development of economic infrastructure such as ports, beaches and roads, which is shared by residents and visitors alike.
• Tourism contributes to improvement of technology in the form of transport and communication.
• Energy infrastructure is needed to operate tourist sites.
• Basic services are required, such as clean water and refuse removal.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does a decline in tourism activities impact on rural communities?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• People in rural areas will have fewer job opportunities, thereby increasing poverty levels.
• People in rural areas may be forced to migrate to urban areas in search of jobs.
• Investment in tourism-related activities (restaurants, hotels) will decline due to decreased demand for goods and services.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the cartoon 'HAZARDOUS WASTE' in the question paper, which depicts toxic waste being dumped.) Name the type of pollution demonstrated in the above cartoon.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Water / sea (pollution) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Give the international measure that deals with the control of hazardous waste.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Basel Convention (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term conservation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
Conservation is the sustainable use and management of the environment to ensure that it can be used by both present and future generations / managing the environment to ensure continuity.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the effect of soil erosion on food security.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Land can no longer be cultivated, thereby leading to a shortage of food supply.
• The loss of topsoil results in higher production costs and an increase in the price of food, thereby making food less affordable.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does human activity negatively affect environmental sustainability?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• Human activity causes environmental degradation, which causes the depletion of resources.
• Directly or indirectly, overpopulation increases damage to the environment.
• Actions taken by humans such as the burning and destruction of forests damage the environment.
• Polluting the environment and depletion of the ozone layer will lead to global warming.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss the reasons why markets fail to ensure environmental sustainability.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained reason (4 x 2 = 8 marks):
• The environment is a common resource / Non-excludability of the environment: Many parts of the environment are not privately owned and do not have a price, so there is no economic incentive for markets to economise on their use.
• Externalities: Because no one person owns the environment, there is no one to enforce property rights over it; when people pollute the environment, the costs are borne mainly by others.
• Lack of knowledge: People may cause environmental damage without realising it, especially when the effects build up over a long time.
• Carelessness / Negligence / Ignorance: Consumers and businesses are frequently prepared to continue with harmful practices and leave future generations to worry about the environmental consequences due to self-interest.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse marketing strategies used to promote tourism in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained strategy). The following marketing strategies have been used to promote tourism:
• launching the Welcome campaign to make every tourist feel at home and encourage them to return for a repeat visit and tell others about their experience.
• introducing Welcome Awards to recognise businesses and individuals that improve the quality of tourist offerings.
• launching the Sho't Left campaign, aimed at making travel more accessible and affordable to encourage South Africans to travel within their country.
• building strong partnerships between SA Tourism and other organisations such as Computicket Travel and Flight Centre in offering South Africans special deals on flights, accommodation and train trips.
• showcasing a wide variety of the best tourism products in South Africa and attracting visitors from across the world through the annual Tourism Indaba.
• establishing the Tourism Enterprise Partnership to improve the sustainability of small tourism enterprises, protect and promote job creation and transform the tourism industry.
• using social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and Twitter to promote tourism.
• launching E-visas, which is likely to attract more tourists.
(Accept the four P's that relate to promotional campaigns, accessibility of places, pricing of tourism products, and tourist attractions and products.)
(Accept any other correct and relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

questions.title: QUESTION 4: MICROECONOMICS AND CONTEMPORARY ECONOMIC ISSUES

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO examples of fixed costs.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Rent
• Administrative costs
• Insurance
• Depreciation
• Salaries
• Interest on capital
• Property taxes
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does the Paris Agreement intend to reduce the impact of climate change?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2 = 2 marks):
• Making finance available to help countries deal with the impact of climate change.
• Intensifying efforts to limit temperature increases (to less than 2 °C) to significantly reduce the risks threatening food production.
• Increasing the ability of countries to adapt to the adverse impacts of climate change.
• Requesting countries to submit strategies on how to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the picture 'WORLD HERITAGE SITES' in the question paper, in which a tourist says: 'I have been all over the world. Visited the Taj Mahal, Tower Bridge and Robben Island. I can't wait to visit some more sites!') Identify ONE World Heritage Site in South Africa in the information above.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Robben Island (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE benefit of tourism for households.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark:
• Enjoy infrastructure
• Skills development
• Income increases
• More job opportunities
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term indigenous knowledge systems.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
The practices and ceremonies that are unique to the country's indigenous (local) people / local knowledge that is unique to a given culture or society / stories and traditions carried over from one generation to the other.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can the depreciation of the rand affect inbound tourism?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Foreign tourists will spend less of their currency to buy rand on the foreign exchange market.
• More foreign tourists will visit the country as it will be cheaper for them to buy goods and services in South Africa.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why do tourists visit South Africa as a tourist destination?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• South Africa offers authenticity and uniqueness for tourists to learn how local people live and work.
• South Africa has a diverse culture for tourists to experience and is known for its friendliness and humility.
• A favourable exchange rate ensures an affordable visit.
• South Africa has favourable climatic conditions for tourists to enjoy different activities.
• South Africa has hosted many international events such as conferences and sporting events.
• The peaceful political transformation of the country to achieve democracy.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the extract 'OLIGOPOLY – COLLUSION IN THE BANKING SECTOR' in the question paper. Three South African banks have been implicated in widespread collusion relating to price fixing of the rand, buying and selling US dollars in exchange for the rand at fixed prices. The competition policy has made provision for the establishment of the Competition Commission, Competition Tribunal and Competition Appeal Court to deal with issues of collusion.) Identify the institution that is responsible for investigating anti-competitive behaviour.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Competition Commission (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: (Refer to the extract in the question paper.) Name the type of collusion explained in the extract above.
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Overt / formal / explicit (collusion) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term oligopoly.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
A market structure dominated by a few large firms.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does the existence of monopolies influence the supply of goods and services?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Monopolies reduce the number of businesses in an industry, reducing the total supply of goods and services.
• Monopolies may restrict the supply of goods and services in order to charge higher prices.
(Accept any other correct and relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: What is the impact of price fixing on the market?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• Consumers may end up paying higher prices for goods and services.
• Businesses may be forced to pay penalties if they are found guilty of price fixing.
• Demand for the product may decrease as customers fail to afford the higher prices.
• Businesses may temporarily enjoy high profits, which may increase supply of the product.
(Accept any other relevant and correct response.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a graph, explain the shutdown point in a perfect market.
subQuestions.memoText:
GRAPH – Shutdown point (Max 4 marks):
• Correct drawing and labelling of cost curves (MC, AC, AVC) = 1 mark
• Correct labelling of axes (Cost, Revenue, Price on the vertical axis; Quantity on the horizontal axis) = 1 mark
• Correct labelling on the axes (P1, P2, P3 and Q1, Q2, Q3) = 1 mark
• Correctly indicating the shutdown point = 1 mark

EXPLANATION (Max 4 marks):
• Above Q1, the firm will continue to produce because the price is greater than AVC, which means the business can pay for all its variable costs.
• Below Q1, the firm will stop producing because the price is less than AVC, which means the firm is no longer able to pay all its variable costs.
• Therefore, point A, where price (AR) is equal to AVC, is the shutdown point.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.) Maximum 4 marks.

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the impact of an increase in the population on the environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). An increase in population will result in:
• demand for food increasing, thereby putting more pressure on the environment.
• deforestation due to increased demand for infrastructure development.
• increased human settlement causing soil erosion and loss of biodiversity.
• increased land and water pollution as more biological and non-biological waste is introduced to the environment.
• depletion of raw materials due to increased production of goods and services.
• resources being severely strained when population increases, e.g. water.
• an increase in the burning of fossil fuels such as coal or petrol due to higher demand for energy.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Essay Question (40 marks – 40 minutes):
• Discuss, in detail, without drawing graphs, state intervention as a consequence of market failure. (26)
• How can market inefficiency be reduced by global markets (globalisation)? (10)

Structure of essay:
- Introduction (Max 2 marks)
- Body: Main Part (Max 26 marks) - max 8 marks for headings/examples
- Body: Additional Part (Max 10 marks) - max 2 marks for mere listing
- Conclusion (Max 2 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
When market failure occurs, consequences such as inefficiencies, spill-over effects, imperfect competition and government intervention are likely to prevail.
(Accept any other correct relevant introduction.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) – State intervention as a consequence of market failure:

DIRECT CONTROL
• The state can pass laws or use existing legislative frameworks to control businesses, industries and individuals who generate negative externalities.
• In South Africa, emissions of potentially dangerous chemicals, air and scenic pollution, and environmental preservation are controlled through various Acts and regulations.
• Advertising by the tobacco industry is prohibited and alcohol may not be sold on Sundays or to persons under the age of 18 years.

IMPERFECT MARKETS
The government can deal with imperfect competition by:
• Formulating or implementing a competition policy to increase the level of competition.
• Using laws on competition to prevent exorbitant prices charged by firms, to ensure that entry to the market is free, prevent harmful collusion and encourage foreign competition which helps to keep prices low.
• Granting licences to more businesses in the case of state monopolies.
• Imposing price controls to decrease prices of goods and services.

LEVYING OF TAXES
• The government will intervene in the market by levying taxes to recover external costs.
• These taxes will increase the price and will result in a decrease in production of a certain good.
• Levying taxes could be used as a strategy of reducing production and consumption of demerit goods as well as generating revenue for the state.
• Firms and consumers will then be allocating resources in a more efficient way.

PROVIDING PRODUCER SUBSIDIES
• The government provides subsidies to producers to encourage them to produce more goods and services.
• Subsidies increase supply of specific goods and services such as milk, wheat and maize.
• Subsidies lower the cost of producing goods and thus the market price of these goods is lowered, increasing consumption.

MINIMUM WAGES
• A minimum wage is the lowest remuneration that employers are required by law to pay their workers.
• Income for the workers will increase and as a result their standard of living will improve (improve welfare and ensure basic needs are met).
• If a minimum wage is set above the equilibrium market wage, supply of labour will exceed the demand for labour.
• This will increase the cost of labour, resulting in higher cost of production for businesses.
• Some workers may be retrenched, increasing unemployment while production decreases.
• Minimum wages will lead to more bargaining power for workers.

MINIMUM PRICES
• The government is obliged to intervene to ensure sufficient supplies of staple food in the market.
• The approach of setting minimum prices or price floors will be used so that it will be worthwhile for producers (to make a comfortable profit) to produce essential goods in desired quantities.
• These are prices that are set above the market price by the government.
• Minimum prices, however, have unwanted side-effects as they cause a surplus in the market.
• Surplus products become a challenge to dispose of, as they should rather be sold at lower costs, dumped in other countries (which is prohibited by the WTO) or destroyed.

MAXIMUM PRICES
• The government will set a maximum price if the price is deemed to be too high for essential (basic) goods.
• The maximum price set by the government below the market price is known as a price ceiling or maximum price.
• The government will intervene in the market by passing a law that suppliers may not charge more than a maximum price.
• The immediate effect of maximum prices in the market is that the quantity supplied drops, thus causing shortages.
• Shortages in supply for certain goods in the market will result in the establishment of 'black markets'.

REDISTRIBUTION OF WEALTH
• The South African government uses a progressive income tax system to redistribute income and wealth.
• Traditional methods such as levying various taxes, provisioning of free services, benefits in kind and cash benefits are used to reduce the income gap.
• The government can also implement redress methods such as BBBEE, affirmative action, land restitution, land redistribution and property subsidies to redistribute wealth among the population.

GOVERNMENT INVOLVEMENT IN PRODUCTION
• Subsidising merit goods to increase production.
• Imposing taxes on demerit goods to reduce production.
• Levying income taxes, indirect taxes and wealth taxes to provide community goods free of charge.
• Providing collective goods such as refuse removal, waste disposal and sewerage drainage for a user fee.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

BODY: ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) – How can market inefficiency be reduced by global markets (globalisation)?
• allowing foreign direct investment in the economy to increase supply of goods and services.
• increasing competition in the local market and reducing the existence of monopolies.
• increasing the accessibility of information to both consumers and producers for them to make rational or informed decisions.
• ensuring efficient allocation of resources by allowing countries to specialise in the production of goods in which they have a comparative advantage.
• increasing mobility of factors of production between different countries.
• encouraging businesses to be innovative and produce goods and services of better quality for consumers.
• increasing consumers' choice of goods and services.
(Accept any other relevant and correct higher-order response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
Market failure may also result in inefficiencies in the way resources are allocated and used in producing goods and services.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion.)

• Discuss the consequences of inflation. (26)
• How does foreign direct investment influence inflation in the economy? (10)

Structure of essay:
- Introduction (Max 2 marks)
- Body: Main Part (Max 26 marks) - max 8 marks for headings/examples

subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
Inflation refers to a sustained and significant increase in the general level of prices over a period of time.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) – Discuss the consequences of inflation:

CREDITORS
• Creditors (lenders) suffer due to price increases because they get money back which has a lower purchasing power, especially if the interest rate has been below the inflation rate / inflation harms creditors as they lose due to a fall in the real value of money.
• Changes in price levels affect debtors and creditors differently at different time periods.

DEBTORS
• Debtors (borrowers) receive money with a high buying power and pay back with money of a lower buying power.
• Borrowers benefit from price increases.
• During periods of rising prices, debtors gain in real terms because the contract was signed in advance and cannot be changed.
• Debtors receive the money with a relatively high purchasing power and repay their loans with low purchasing power, unless interest rates are sufficient to prevent the situation.

SALARY AND WAGE EARNERS
• Price increases affect people negatively because their incomes are relatively fixed.
• Real wages fall sharply during periods of high inflation as a result of a decline in capital stock and a shift in relative prices.
• Inflation can impoverish large segments of the population by eroding real wages.
• Relative wages are an important component of wealth; they constitute the main source of income for many households, especially the less well-off.
• The behaviour of real wages therefore has a direct bearing on income distribution and the level of poverty.
• This group includes retired people, pensioners and the poor, who will experience the erosion of spending power and eventually earn too little to survive.
• Wage increases are lower than the inflation rate increase.

INVESTORS AND SAVERS
• Assets with a fixed nominal value have a fixed return and lower purchasing power as prices increase.
• Purchasing power is reduced unless the interest rate is above the inflation rate.
• People who invest in negotiable instruments such as shares often benefit from inflation, because during periods of inflation interest rates are increased to encourage savings.
• Investors in assets with flexible market value gain when prices increase, because their assets increase at least proportionately to the rate of inflation.
• Often the prices of these assets increase more rapidly than increases in the general price level.
• People save money for long periods with the aim of using these funds to meet future expectations; these savings may be invested as fixed deposits, in the money market, as life policies or in pension funds.

TAX PAYERS
• With inflation, taxpayers' nominal income rises although their real income remains unchanged, because taxes are levied on nominal income and not on real income, and this affects the purchasing power of taxpayers.
• Taxes are levied on nominal income and not on real income.
• If the income tax brackets remain unchanged, inflation increases the average rate of personal income tax.
• Individuals will have to pay higher taxes even if they are actually no better off than before – bracket creep leads to a redistribution of income from taxpayers to the government.

INDUSTRIAL PEACE
• Wage bargaining is accompanied by strikes and mass action.
• These actions can sometimes spill over into violence which affects society at large.
• Inflation leads to demands for increased wages as trade unions put increasing pressure on employers to raise wages and salaries.
• In extreme situations, exceptionally high inflation together with a government determined not to yield to wage-increase demands (which can push inflation to even higher levels) can lead to widespread civil unrest.

BALANCE OF PAYMENTS
• If a country's rate of inflation is higher than that of its trading partners, the prices of exported goods increase while the prices of imported goods decrease.
• This leads to loss of competitiveness in the export market, leading to a decrease in exports.
• Cheaper imports have a negative effect on a country's balance of payments.
• The loss of competitiveness can result in increased unemployment.

UNEMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY
• The effects of inflation are uneven, because it does not benefit anyone and harms most – some less than others.
• Inflation also tends to redistribute income from low-income groups to higher-income groups.
• This is because people in the low-income groups do not have assets that can rise in value faster than the rate of inflation to help them overcome the effects of inflation.
• Powerful groups such as trade unions, large companies and wealthy people are able to increase their share of national income at the expense of disadvantaged people such as pensioners, the unemployed and welfare recipients.

PSYCHOLOGICAL INFLUENCE
Low inflation expectations:
• limit excessive wage demands by labour unions because workers do not expect increases in the cost of living in the future.
• allow consumers to postpone consumption expenditure, thereby reducing pressure on price increases.
• give households confidence that the inflation rate will be low in future and encourage them to save more of their income, thereby controlling excess demand.
• reduce panic buying by consumers when they expect prices to be stable in the future.
• boost real interest rates which will encourage savings.
• increase the burden on debtors, which discourages them from borrowing money due to the real interest rate.
High inflation expectations:
• excessive wage demands by labour unions because workers anticipate increases in the cost of living, leading producers to increase prices to recover extra costs of production.
• prompt consumers to engage in panic buying when they expect prices to rise, thereby increasing pressure on prices to rise.
• make households save less, thereby leading to excess demand for goods and services.
• decrease real interest rates, which will discourage savings.
• reduce the burden on creditors as they will receive their money at higher interest rates.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 8 marks may be allocated for headings/examples.)

BODY: ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) – How does foreign direct investment influence inflation in the economy?
Foreign direct investment influences inflation in the economy by:
• increasing the production of goods and services which will increase aggregate supply, thus stabilising prices.
• bringing more efficient production techniques that will reduce production costs, slowing down cost-push inflation.
• increasing competition in local markets which will keep local prices low.
• strengthening the rand through higher export volumes, which helps to reduce the cost of importing production inputs such as crude oil.
• improving technology in production which increases productivity, thereby reducing cost-push inflation.
• creating more employment opportunities, thereby stimulating consumer spending which contributes to demand-pull inflation.
• increasing expenditure on capital goods such as machinery and equipment, resulting in increased aggregate demand.
• increasing real wages more than domestic investment, leading to cost-push inflation.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
Unacceptably high inflation rates cause hardships among the poor, the unemployed and low-income earners; proper measures to control it have to be put in place.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order response.)
